Offline Draft Sync

A draft written without a connection is saved on the device, and the save has to wait for a pause in the typing rather than firing on every keystroke. Three ways to hold it back.

This is sample content. Every region of this document is a worked example built on the invented feature NIMBUS-101, and each one is waiting to be filled with a real feature.

Approaches

Each approach carries its own anchor, so the one you choose travels with the export instead of being restated in prose. Read the trade-offs, then choose one.

Which approach should this change take?

Inline timer in the editor

The delay lives directly inside the component that owns the draft field.

export function DraftEditor() {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState('');
  const [settled, setSettled] = useState('');

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setSettled(draft), 300);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);
  }, [draft]);

  useLocalDraft({ body: settled });

  return (
    <textarea
      value={draft}
      onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)}
      placeholder="Write your draft…"
    />
  );
}
Trade-offs for the inline timer
Pro Con
+No new abstraction for a reviewer to learn −The same timer is rewritten wherever a draft is edited
+Easy to step through when a save goes missing −Two pieces of state for one draft body
+No dependency and no bundle change −The pause length is buried in the component
  • Bundle impact: +0 kb
  • Testability: medium
  • Reuse: low
  • Offline safe: yes

Shared debounce hook

The timer moves into one hook under src/hooks/ that every draft surface imports.

// src/hooks/useDebounce.ts
export function useDebounce<T>(value: T, ms = 300): T {
  const [settled, setSettled] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setSettled(value), ms);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);
  }, [value, ms]);
  return settled;
}

// DraftEditor.tsx
const [draft, setDraft] = useState('');
const settled = useDebounce(draft, 300);
useLocalDraft({ body: settled });
Trade-offs for the shared hook
Pro Con
+One import serves the editor, the outbox note, and the conflict prompt −One more file to maintain and document
+Unit tests run it against fake timers in isolation −The generic type hides what is being held back
+The pause length is a visible, tunable argument −The editor still re-renders on every keystroke
  • Bundle impact: +0.2 kb
  • Testability: high
  • Reuse: high
  • Offline safe: yes

Third-party debounce library

Adopt use-debounce for both the value and the save callback.

import { useDebouncedCallback }
  from 'use-debounce';

export function DraftEditor() {
  const [settled, setSettled] = useState('');

  const onChange = useDebouncedCallback(
    (next: string) => setSettled(next),
    300,
    { leading: false, maxWait: 1000 },
  );

  useLocalDraft({ body: settled });

  return (
    <textarea
      defaultValue=""
      onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}
Trade-offs for the library
Pro Con
+A ceiling on the wait, so a fast typist still gets a save −A new runtime dependency to audit and update
+The callback form skips the intermediate re-renders −An uncontrolled field diverges from the rest of the editor
+Unmount, flush, and cancel are already covered −Roughly 1.4 kb for something a ten-line hook does
  • Bundle impact: +1.4 kb
  • Testability: high
  • Reuse: high
  • Offline safe: yes

Recommendation

What planning chose, and what would reopen the question.

Go with the shared debounce hook. Three surfaces already hand-roll the inline timer — the draft editor, the outbox note field, and the conflict prompt — so extracting one hook removes the duplication without taking on a dependency, and it leaves the pause length as an argument the flag ramp can tune.

Revisit the third-party library only if the replay work later needs maxWait or flush(). A draft that never settles because the author never pauses is a real failure mode, and it is the one thing a ten-line hook does not answer.
